prompt: Name one of Santa's reindeer, including Rudolph.
source: Clement Clarke Moore, 'A Visit from St. Nicholas' (1823), plus Robert L. May's 1939 Rudolph.
valueLogic: Rudolph is free - he is in the title of the song. Dasher, Dancer and Prancer come as a rhyming group. Blitzen and Vixen are distinctive enough to stick. Donner, Comet and Cupid are the tail: Comet and Cupid especially, because they are the only two that are neither motion words nor part of a rhyme.
note: Donder, Dunder and Blixem are the poem's own spellings, so they're aliases worth the same points. Olive and Clarice are later inventions and non-busting distractors.

answers.name: Rudolph
answers.fact: Invented in 1939 for a Montgomery Ward promotional booklet, not in the original poem.

answers.name: Dasher
answers.fact: First named in the poem, and the first of the eight listed.

answers.name: Prancer
answers.fact: Third, and rhymes with Dancer, which is why people recall them as a pair.

answers.name: Blitzen
answers.fact: Blixem in the 1823 original - Dutch for lightning.

answers.name: Vixen
answers.fact: Fourth in the poem, and the only one named for an animal - a vixen is a female fox.

answers.name: Donner
answers.fact: Dunder in the 1823 poem and Donder in Moore's later version - Dutch for thunder, paired with Blitzen's lightning.

answers.name: Comet
answers.fact: Fifth in the poem, and the only one named for something in space.

answers.name: Cupid
answers.fact: Sixth, and the hardest of the nine. The only one named after a god.

distractors.name: Olive
distractors.note: From the mishearing of 'all of the other reindeer' - a joke, not a reindeer.

distractors.name: Clarice
distractors.note: Rudolph's friend in the 1964 television special, and not one of the nine.

distractors.name: Fireball
distractors.note: From the 1964 special, not the poem.

distractors.name: Sven
distractors.note: From Frozen, and not one of Santa's.

distractors.name: Olaf
distractors.note: A snowman, and from a different story entirely.
